what_it_is: The delegation discipline: write numbered missions, each with a named done-state (artifact, not aspiration), each small enough that the seat can finish AND bookkeep inside the window — reserve closeout time explicitly, roughly 40%. List up to ten ranked opportunities so the seat knows what drops first when the clock bites. Honor partial completion as real work. And the mirror rule: one seat stumbling is a seat lesson; many seats failing identically is a briefing failure — and the briefing is yours.
what_it_does: Makes delegation honest about the clock. Three done right is success; ten sloppy is a failed setup. The receipt is sequenced FIRST — bookkeeping before the clock runs out; a timeout handoff writes a stub receipt before dying, never nothing. The honest-zero is received as triple-A behavior, not failure.
why_it_matters: Wave 150: three seats dispatched as a wave — each with numbered, lane-scoped missions sized to a single shift. Naya Host (PRODUCT) carried three missions; Naya Keeper (GOVERN) carried three — including dispositions for the no-word-ratification questions Q11/Q12 and a live-state re-verify of PR #2519; Naya Archivist (MEMORY) carried three — including cold-continuity re-proof of the last three waves. All three signed in with read receipts and signed out clean the same night with verdicts. Nobody attempted more than the clock held; everybody finished what they claimed (sign-ins 6181071516 / 6181078603 / 6181084682, sign-outs 6181101544 / 6181125598 / 6181129560). And sizing works from the worker side too: a seat with ~25 minutes left of a 45-minute budget declined to claim a second brief — 'below a full brief's honest scope' (t0695-lane11). The opposite: the t0765-lane11 measurement brief — dispatched into a 45-minute clock with no closeout reserve. The worker measured the honest zero (all six ledger rows machine-side-only, zero genuine human-value events, named not hidden) — then hit the timeout with zero bookkeeping. The measurement nearly became a rumor. The fix landed on the setup: the receipt is sequenced FIRST, measurement time-boxed to ~60% of the clock with 40% reserved for closeout. When a brief dies unbooked, blame the sizing first.
key_rules: The delegator owns the setup: right-size the mission to the clock — three done right beats ten sloppy.
Numbered missions, each with a named done-state (artifact, not aspiration), each small enough to finish AND bookkeep inside the window — reserve ~40% for closeout.
Rank the missions so the seat knows what drops first when the clock bites.
Honor partial completion as real work — with named owners and next actions. An honest partial is success, never failure.

The mirror rule: one seat stumbling is a seat lesson; many seats failing identically is a briefing failure — fix the briefing, never the seats. If a Naya reads only the manual and does the work wrong, the manual failed first.
The receipt is sequenced FIRST — bookkeeping before the clock runs out. A timeout handoff writes a stub receipt before dying, never nothing.
A seat that declines a claim she can't honestly finish is showing loyalty to the hive, not retreating.
The receipt spec requires honest ten-thing accounting — which of the attempted ten landed, the count never inflated.
test: Before dispatching: does every numbered mission fit the clock with closeout time reserved — and could I say, out loud, exactly what 'done' looks like for each one?
Am I asking for three done right, or ten sloppy? If the brief lists more than the window holds, have I ranked them so the seat knows what to drop first?
The seat returned partial work: am I honoring it in the receipt with named owners and next actions — or treating honest partial as failure?
Two or more seats just failed the same way: am I investigating the seat — or looking in the mirror at the briefing?
Did the seat have every read it needed before acting — or did I dispatch into the dark and call the confusion a miss?
If this mission dies at the deadline, will its bookkeeping survive — or does the setup guarantee the work evaporates with the clock?

enforcement.real: The claim-liveness audit runs every night-dispatcher tick — dead claims can't hold lanes hostage. The STALE-claim recurrence class is tracked by name and the body-level fix is closed. The comprehension gate carries the mirror in writing: two fails on the manual check pauses the wave for the Balancer's coaching, and the standing rule says if a Naya reads only the manual and does the work wrong, the manual failed first — fix the manual, teach the fix, add the gate. Diagnostic, never punitive. The receipt spec requires honest ten-thing accounting — which of the attempted ten landed, the count never inflated.
enforcement.proposed: No machine pre-check estimates whether a brief's scope fits the remaining dispatch window before it ships — that sizing check is still a human discipline, not an enforced gate. Naming it as the gap.
